What Cellular Reproduction Accomplishes

  • Reproduction may result in the birth of new organisms, but more commonly involves the production of new cells.
  • When a cell undergoes reproduction, or cell division, two “daughter” cells are produced that are genetically identical to each other and the “parent” cell.
  • Before a parent cell splits into two, it duplicates its chromosomes, the structures that contain most of the cell’s DNA.
  • Cell division plays several important roles in the lives of organisms. Cell division
    • replaces damaged or lost cells,
    • permits growth, and
    • allows for reproduction.
  • Mitosis is the type of cell division responsible for
    • asexual reproduction and
    • growth and maintenance of multicellular organisms.
  • In asexual reproduction, single-celled organisms reproduce by dividing in half, producing offspring that are genetic replicas of the parent cell.
  • Sexual reproduction requires fertilization of an egg by a sperm.
    • The production of gametes—egg and sperm—involves a special type of cell division called meiosis, which occurs only in reproductive organs.

The Cell Cycle and Mitosis

  • In a eukaryotic cell, most genes are located on chromosomes in the cell nucleus, except for genes on small DNA molecules found in mitochondria and chloroplasts.
    • Each eukaryotic chromosome contains one very long DNA molecule, typically bearing thousands of genes.
    • The number of chromosomes in a eukaryotic cell depends on the species.
Text description of this image

The details of the graph are as follows: The x-axis shows the number of chromosomes in body cells. The y-axis shows the various species. The results of the graph are as follows:

Indian muntjac deer: 6 chromosomes; Koala: 16 chromosomes; Opossum: 22 chromosomes; Giraffe: 30 chromosomes; Mouse: 40 chromosomes; Human: 46 chromosomes; Duck-billed platypus: 54 chromosomes; Bison: 60 chromosomes; Dog: 78 chromosomes; Red viscacha rat: 102 chromosomes

Eukaryotic Chromosome

  • Chromosomes are made of chromatin, fibers composed of roughly equal amounts of DNA and protein molecules.
  • The protein molecules help organize the chromatin and help control the activity of its genes.
  • Most of the time, the chromosomes exist as thin fibers that are much longer than the nucleus, they are stored in.
  • The DNA in a chromosome is packed into an elaborate, multilevel system of coiling and folding.
Text description of this image

A light micrograph at a magnification of 1400 shows rows of rectangular plant cells, with chromosomes visible as thick, dark lines labeled in one cell.

Text description of this image

The figure shows the DNA double helix as a twisted, helical structure. It is shown wound around spherical histone proteins and the units of DNA wrapped around the clusters of histone molecules are called nucleosomes. Nucleosomes resemble beads on a string in a corresponding transmission electron micrograph at a magnification of 130,000. Nucleosomes are further twisted and folded into the final chromosome package. A micrograph of a duplicated chromosome (sister chromatids) at a magnification of 9,000 shows two thick, fuzzy, long rods side-by-side, pinched together at a cinched-in region called the centromere.

Duplicating Chromosomes

  • Before a cell begins the division process,
    • the DNA molecule of each chromosome is copied through the process of DNA replication and
    • new histone protein molecules attach as needed.
  • The result is that each chromosome consists of two copies called sister chromatids, which contain identical genes.
  • Two sister chromatids are joined together tightly at a narrow “waist” called the centromere.
  • When the cell divides, the sister chromatids of a duplicated chromosome separate from each other.
  • Once separated from its sister, each chromatid
    • is considered a full-fledged chromosome and
    • is identical to the original chromosome.
Text description of this image

A figure shows a chromosome duplicating into sister chromatids, which are held tightly together until they are separated into two individual chromosomes during chromosome distribution to daughter cells.

Mitosis

Text description of this image

Interphase; Interphase is the period of cell growth when the cell makes new molecules and organelles. At the point shown here, late interphase (G2), the cytoplasm contains two centrosomes. Within the nucleus, the chromosomes are duplicated, but they cannot be distinguished individually because they are still in the form of loosely packed chromatin fibers.; The figure shows a cell with the plasma membrane labeled. The nuclear envelope wraps around the uncondensed chromosomes, which are not discernible in the micrograph. Centrosomes are drawn in the cytoplasm near the nucleus.; A micrograph shows visible long green fibers on one side of the nucleus.; Prophase; During prophase, changes occur in both nucleus and cytoplasm. In the nucleus, the chromatin fibers coil, so that the chromosomes become thick enough to be seen individually with a light microscope. Each chromosome exists as two identical sister chromatids joined together at the narrow waist of the centromere. In the cytoplasm, the mitotic spindle begins to form. Late in prophase, the nuclear envelope breaks into pieces. The spindle tracks attach to the centromeres of the chromosomes and move the chromosomes toward the center of the cell.; Early prophase. Thick lines (chromosomes) are visible in the nucleus in the micrograph, but they blend together. The centrosomes begin to spread out as the mitotic spindle forms, but remain on one side of the nucleus. The figure shows four duplicated chromosomes (sister chromatids) are drawn in the nucleus. Each set of sister chromatids are joined at the centromere. The nuclear envelope is beginning to break down.; Late prophase. The micrograph shows individual chromosomes that are now discernible as thick lines. The mitotic spindle spreads across the cell and reaches both poles. The nuclear envelope has fragmented, and each of the four duplicated chromosomes (sister chromatids) is attached to the spindle tracks at the centromere.

Text description of this image

Metaphase; The mitotic spindle is now fully formed. The centromeres of all the chromosomes line up between the two poles of the spindle. For each chromosome, the tracks of the mitotic spindle attached to the two sister chromatids pull toward opposite poles. This tug of war keeps the chromosomes in the middle of the cell.; The figure shows the four duplicated chromosomes line up end-to-end at the middle of the cell, with one chromatid from each duplicated chromosome oriented toward the opposite pole of the cell. The tracks of the mitotic spindle are attached to each sister chromatid at the centromere. The mitotic spindle is clearly attached to the duplicated chromosomes at the middle of the cell in the micrograph.; Anaphase; Anaphase begins suddenly when the sister chromatids of each chromosome separate. Each is now considered a full-fledged (daughter) chromosome. The chromosomes move toward opposite poles of the cell as the spindle tracks shorten. Simultaneously, the tracks not attached to chromosomes lengthen, pushing the poles farther apart and elongating the cell.; The figure shows the sister chromatids are now separated into individual chromosomes as each half of each of the four duplicated chromosomes moves toward opposite poles of the cell on a track of the mitotic spindle. The chromosomes appear separated in the micrograph.; Telophase; Telophase begins when the two groups of chromosomes have reached opposite ends of the cell. Telophase is the reverse of prophase: Nuclear envelopes form, the chromosomes uncoil, and the spindle disappears. Mitosis, the division of one nucleus into two genetically identical daughter nuclei, is now finished. Cytokinesis, the division of the cytoplasm, usually occurs with telophase. In animals, a cleavage furrow pinches the cell in two, producing two daughter cells.; The figure shows the cell as with a cleavage furrow beginning to separate what will become the two new daughter cells. In each are four chromosomes; the nuclear envelope is reforming around the chromosomes in both cells. The mitotic spindle has retracted. In the micrograph, the constricting mitotic spindle is discernible, as are the two distinct nuclei in the two daughter cells. They are still joined, with a pinched-in region between them.

Cytokinesis

Animals

Plants

Text description of this image

A scanning electron micrograph at a magnification of 100 shows an animal cell cinched inward in the middle by a cleavage furrow, which resembles the pinching-in caused by a drawstring.; An image shows a cleavage furrow as a result of a contracting ring of microfilaments between two forming daughter cells, each with its own distinct nucleus. Two separate daughter cells result following cytokinesis.

A light micrograph at a magnification of 640 shows plant cells undergoing cytokinesis. The wall of the parent cell is visible as a thick line. At each pole of the parent cell is a daughter nucleus. Cancer Cells: Dividing Out of Control

  • The sequential events of the cell cycle are directed by a cell cycle control system that consists of specialized proteins within the cell.
  • Cancer is a disease of the cell cycle.
  • Cancer cells do not respond normally to the cell cycle control system, divide excessively, and may invade other tissues of the body.
  • The abnormal behavior of cancer cells begins when a single cell undergoes genetic changes (mutations) in one or more genes that encode for proteins in the cell cycle control system.
  • Cancer cells can form tumors, abnormally growing masses of body cells.
    • If the abnormal cells remain at the original site, the lump is called a benign tumor.
    • Malignant tumors can spread into neighboring tissues and other parts of the body, forming new tumors, and can interrupt organ function.
      • A person with a malignant tumor is said to have cancer.
      • The spread of cancer cells beyond their original site is called metastasis.
Text description of this image

The figure shows that a tumor grows, invades neighboring tissue, and then spreads to distant parts of the body during metastasis. A tumor can be seen growing from a single cancer cell on the glandular tissue. Cancer cells then invade neighboring tissue. This leads to metastasis: cancer cells spread through the lymph and blood vessels to other parts of the body, forming tumors in distant parts of the body.

Sexual Reproduction and Variability

Meiosis – The Basis of Sexual Reproduction

  • Sexual reproduction
    • produces offspring that contain a unique combination of genes from the parents and
    • depends on the cellular processes of meiosis and fertilization.
  • Different individuals of a single species have the same number and types of chromosomes.
  • A human somatic cell is a typical body cell and has 46 chromosomes.
  • Homologous chromosomes
    • resemble each other in length and centromere position and
    • carry genes controlling the same inherited characteristics.
Text description of this image

The figure shows that each homologous pair consists of chromosomes of the same length and with matching color bands (with the exception of the X and Y chromosomes; the Y chromosome is much shorter than X and does not have matching color bands). An exploded drawing of homologous chromosomes (pair 1) shows that each member of the pair is a duplicated chromosome, which consists of sister chromatids joined at the centromere.

The Human Life Cycle

Humans are diploid organisms because all body cells contain pairs of homologous chromosomes. (A haploid cell has only one member of each pair of homologous chromosomes.)

In the human life cycle, a haploid sperm fuses with a haploid egg in a process called fertilization.

The resulting fertilized egg, called a zygote, is diploid, with two sets of chromosomes, one set of chromosomes from each parent.

Producing haploid gametes by meiosis keeps the chromosome number from doubling in every generation.

Text description of this image

The figure shows that human gametes are produced via meiosis from diploid cells, while development occurs via mitosis after fertilization of the gametes produces a diploid zygote. Multicellular diploid in adults (2n equals 46; a man and a woman are pictured) produce haploid gametes via meiosis (a large egg cell for the woman and a small sperm cell for the man; n equals 23 for both). The sperm and egg fuse during fertilization, producing the diploid zygote (2n equals 46). Mitosis and development occur in the diploid zygote, producing the multicellular diploid adult (and the cycle can begin again).

Meiosis and Chromosome Number

Text description of this image

The figure shows that through meiosis, a diploid parent cell produces four haploid daughter cells. The figure shows that during interphase (before meiosis) a diploid parent cell has one pair of homologous chromosomes (one maternal and one paternal chromosome make up the pair). The figure shows the following steps: 1. Interphase. The chromosomes duplicate, so that the parent cell still contains a pair of homologous chromosomes, but now each chromosome is in sister chromatid form. 2. Meiosis 1. The homologous chromosomes separate, with the maternal duplicated chromosome (in sister chromatid form) going to one daughter cell and the paternal duplicated chromosome (sister chromatids) going to a second daughter cell. 3. Meiosis 2. Sister chromatids separate. Both daughter cells from step 2 divide, with the maternal sister chromatids separating and one copy of the maternal chromosome going to each of two daughter cells; the paternal chromatids also separate into two cells, so that one copy of the paternal chromosome goes into each of two daughter cells. The final result is four haploid daughter cells, each with one chromosome (two cells with maternal copies and two cells with paternal copies).

Stages of Meiosis

Text description of this image

The stage 1 shows the following steps:

Interphase (before meiosis begins); As with mitosis, meiosis is preceded by an interphase during which the chromosomes duplicate. Each chromosome then consists of two identical sister chromatids. The chromosomes consist of uncondensed chromatin fibers. Chromosomes duplicate. A cell is drawn with centrosomes near the nucleus. The nuclear envelope is intact and surrounds uncondensed chromosomes, which exist as a tangle of diffuse fibers.

Text description of this image

Meiosis 1: homologous chromosomes separate; Prophase 1

As the chromosomes coil up, special proteins cause the homologous chromosomes to stick together in pairs. The resulting structure has four chromatids. Within each set, chromatids of the homologous chromosomes exchange corresponding segments—they cross over. Crossing over rearranges genetic information. As prophase 1 continues, the chromosomes coil up further, a spindle forms, and the homologous pairs are moved toward the center of the cell. The Homologous chromosomes pair up and exchange segments. The spindle is beginning to form near the nucleus, which is surrounded by a fragmented nuclear envelope. The figure shows that two pairs of homologous chromosomes are paired and there is a long pair and a short pair in duplicated. Each is composed of maternal (red) and paternal (blue) sister chromatids; part or parts of one maternal chromatid overlaps with one of the paternal chromatids from its homologous pair. These are sites of crossing over.

Metaphase 1

At metaphase 1, the homologous pairs are aligned in the middle of the cell. The sister chromatids of each chromosome are still attached at their centromeres, where they are anchored to spindle tracks. Notice that for each chromosome pair, the spindle tracks attached to one homologous chromosome come from one pole of the cell, and the tracks attached to the other chromosome come from the opposite pole. With this arrangement, the homologous chromosomes are poised to move toward opposite poles of the cell. The figure shows that pairs of homologous chromosomes line up. The short homologous chromosomes are side by side at the center of the cell; as are the long pair of homologous chromosomes. In this alignment, the short maternal duplicated chromosome is lined up adjacent to the long paternal duplicated chromosome, while the short paternal chromosome is adjacent to the long maternal chromosome. Spindle tracks are attached to the centromere of each sister chromatid. There is no nuclear envelope.

Anaphase 1

The attachment between the homologous chromosomes of each pair breaks, and the chromosomes now migrate toward the poles of the cell. In contrast to mitosis, the sister chromatids migrate as a pair instead of splitting up. They are separated not from each other but from their homologous partners. The figure shows that pairs of homologous chromosomes split up. One pair of short and one pair of long sister chromatids move toward each pole of the cell on the spindle tracks. Sister chromatids move together, remaining attached to each other and to the spindle track at the centromere. In this alignment, the short maternal sister chromatids and the long paternal sister chromatids move to one cell pole (on separate spindle tracks), while the short paternal and long maternal sister chromatids move to the opposite cell pole (also on different spindle tracks). There is a segment of blue on one maternal chromatid from each homologous pair, and a segment of red on one paternal chromatid of each pair, indicating that crossing over has occurred and the stage two shows the following steps:

Meiosis 1; Telophase 1 and cytokinesis

In telophase 1, the chromosomes arrive at the poles of the cell. When they finish their journey, each pole has a haploid chromosome set, although each chromosome is still in duplicate form. Usually, cytokinesis occurs along with telophase 1, and two haploid daughter cells are formed. The figure shows the two haploid cell forms; chromosomes are still doubled. A cell can be seen in the process of dividing into two cells; there is a pinched-in region between the two cells (the cleavage furrow). The nuclear envelope is reforming around each new daughter nucleus. In this alignment, one new nucleus contains the long paternal sister chromatids and the short maternal chromatids; the other new nucleus contains the long maternal sister chromatids and the short paternal sister chromatids. Color exchanges on one arm of one chromatid of each pair represent the crossing over that occurred during prophase 1.

Text description of this image

Meiosis 2; The Process of Meiosis 2: Meiosis 2 is essentially the same as mitosis. The important difference is that meiosis 2 starts with a haploid cell that has not undergone chromosome duplication during the preceding interphase.; Prophase 2

A spindle forms and moves the chromosomes toward the middle of the cell. There are two separate cells; the nuclear envelope is fragmented in each. One nucleus contains the short maternal and long paternal chromatids; the other contains the short paternal and long maternal chromatids. (There are no homologous pairs in the same cell). The spindle is constricted. During prophase 2, a spindle forms and moves the chromosomes toward the middle of the cell.

Metaphase 2

During metaphase 2, the chromosomes are aligned as they are in mitosis, with the tracks attached to the sister chromatids of each chromosome coming from opposite poles. The chromosomes are aligned in the middle of the cell as they are in mitosis, with the tracks attached to the sister chromatids of each chromosome coming from opposite poles. The sister chromatids are lined up end to end at the middle of both daughter cells. The spindle has reformed and spindle tracks attach to the centromere of the short sister chromatids and the long sister chromatids in each cell.

Anaphase 2; The centromeres of sister chromatids separate, and the sister chromatids of each pair move toward opposite poles of the cell. Spindle fibers pull one short and one long chromosome toward the poles of each cell. Sister chromatids are separated into individual chromosomes.; In anaphase II, the centromeres of sister chromatids separate, and the sister chromatids of each pair move toward opposite poles of the cell. In telophase II, nuclei form at the cell poles, and cytokinesis occurs at the same time. There are now four haploid daughter cells, each with single chromosomes.; During another round of cell division, the sister chromatids finally separate; four haploid daughter cells result, containing single chromosomes.; Telophase 2 and cytokinesis; Nuclei form at the cell poles, and cytokinesis occurs at the same time. There are now four haploid daughter cells, each with single chromosomes.; The figure shows two cells are nearly finished dividing into the four final daughter cells. Nuclear envelopes are reforming and the spindle is constricted. The four haploid daughter cells will each contain one long and one short chromosome.

Rearranging Chromosomes

Text description of this image

Two equally probable arrangements of chromosomes at metaphase of meiosis 1.; Parent Cell with 2 pairs of duplicated homologous chromosomes (long and short). Homologous pairs line up at the middle of the cell to be separated.; Possibility 1: Long paternal sister chromatids line up above short paternal sister chromatids; long maternal sister chromatids line up above short maternal sister chromatids; Possibility 2: Long paternal sister chromatids line up above short maternal sister chromatids; long maternal sister chromatids line up above short paternal sister chromatids; Metaphase of meiosis 2:; 2 daughter cells each with one long and one short set of sister chromatids; Possibility 1

§ Cell 1: Long paternal sister chromatids line up above short paternal sister chromatids in middle of cell. § Cell 2: Long maternal sister chromatids line up above short maternal sister chromatids in the center of cell.

Possibility 2:

§ Cell 1: Long paternal sister chromatids line up above short maternal sister chromatids in the middle of cell. § Cell 2: long maternal sister chromatids line up above short paternal sister chromatids in middle of cell.

Gametes; 4 haploid daughter cells show four combinations of gametes. Because possibilities one and two (alignment at metaphase I) are equally likely, the four possible types of gametes will be made in approximately equal numbers.; Possibility 1: Combination a (2 cells): Long paternal chromosome and short paternal chromosome. Combination b (2 cells): Long maternal chromosome and short maternal chromosome.; Possibility 2: Combination c (2 cells): long paternal chromosome, short maternal chromosome. Combination d (2 cells): short paternal chromosome, long maternal chromosome.

When Meiosis Makes Oversights

Text description of this image

Meiosis 1; Nondisjunction: Pairs of homologues chromosomes fail to separate. The figure shows that cell has two pairs of homologous chromosomes (long and short) in sister chromatid form. The short pair separates normally, but the long pair sticks together and moves toward one pole of the cell on the spindle track.; Normal: The figure shows that cell has two pairs of homologous chromosomes (long and short) in sister chromatid form. Both the long and short homologous pairs separate normally, with sister chromatids moving together toward the pole opposite their homologue on the spindle track.; Meiosis 2; Proceeds normally. The figure shows that two daughter cells result from meiosis 1: one with three sets of sister chromatids and the other with only one set. All sister chromatids separate in both cells.; Nondisjunction: The sister chromatids fail to separate. In one daughter cell, the short sister chromatids separate normally, but the long sister chromatids stick together and move together toward one pole of the cell. In the second daughter cell, meiosis 2 is normal and both sets of sister chromatids separate normally.; Gametes; All four gametes are abnormal. The figure shows that two gametes are n plus 1 (contain three chromosomes in this example) and two are n-1 (contain one chromosome).; Two abnormal and two normal gametes are produced. One gamete is n+1 with three chromosomes (abnormal); one gamete is n minus 1 with 1 chromosome (abnormal); and two normal gametes are each n with two chromosomes.

Text description of this image

The figure shows that a normal haploid sperm cell (n) carries two chromosomes. The sperm fertilizes an abnormal egg cell that has an extra chromosome (n plus 1), and carries three chromosomes. Fertilization results in an abnormal zygote with one extra chromosome (2n plus 1). The zygote has five chromosomes, two from the sperm cell and three from the egg cell.

Trisomy 21 and Down Syndrome

  • In a condition called trisomy 21, there are three number 21 chromosomes, making 47 chromosomes in total.
  • A person with trisomy 21 has a condition called Down syndrome, which
    • affects about 1 out of every 850 children,
    • is the most common chromosome number abnormality, and
    • is the most common serious birth defect in the United States.
Text description of this image

A photo shows a child with Down syndrome and a light micrograph of a karyotype at a magnification of 4,000 showing 22 pairs of chromosomes and two X chromosomes. At chromosome 21, there are three chromosomes instead of two which is labeled as trisomy 21.

Comparing Mitosis and Meiosis

Text description of this image

Mitosis; Prophase

Chromosome duplication occurs during the preceding interphase. The figure shows a cell with 4 duplicated chromosomes (sister chromatids) in the cell. There is one long maternal (red), one long paternal (blue), one short maternal and one short paternal duplicated chromosome.

Metaphase

Individual chromosomes align at the middle of the cell, end to end. Each is on a spindle track.

Anaphase and telophase

Sister chromatids separate during anaphase, producing 2 daughter cells that are diploid (2n). Each daughter cell from mitosis contains one long maternal (red), one long paternal (blue), one short maternal and one short paternal chromosome.

Meiosis; Prophase 1

Chromosome duplication occurs during the preceding interphase. Homologous chromosomes come together in pairs, so that the long maternal and paternal duplicated chromosomes are side by side, as are the short maternal and paternal chromosomes (also in sister chromatid form). Where the nonsister chromatids overlap is the site of crossing over between homologous (nonsister) chromatids. In the drawing, one blue chromatid and one red chromatid from each pair overlap.

Metaphase 1

Homologous pairs align at the middle of the cell. In this example, the short and long maternal sister chromatids are lined up on the left side of the cell end to end on a spindle track, while their homologous pair (the short and long paternal sister chromatids) are beside them.

Anaphase 1 and telophase 1

Daughter cells of meiosis 1

Homologous chromosomes separate during anaphase I; sister chromatids remain attached. Two haploid daughter cells result (n=2); one contains the short and long maternal chromosomes with two sister chromatids each; the other contains the long and short paternal chromosomes with two sister chromatids each. These are the daughter cells of meiosis 1. Blue color segments on one maternal chromatid for each pair, and red segments on one paternal chromatid from each pair symbolize that crossing over has occurred.

Daughter cells of meiosis 2

Sister chromatids separate during anaphase II, producing four haploid daughter cells (n). Each contains one long and one short unduplicated chromosome. Two cells contain long and short maternal chromosomes and two contain the long and short paternal chromosomes. Crossing over has occurred.
